lines: A pulse oscillator built as two 555 timer chips would be wired, one running free and triggering the other, whose pulse length is set in milliseconds rather than as a fraction of the cycle
Sets the frequency of the free-running oscillator, four octaves either side of C4
Sets how long the output stays high after each trigger, 0.1ms to 20ms, which changes the timbre without changing the rate
Shifts the frequency by 0.8 octaves per volt, added to the frequency knob and clamped to four octaves either side of C4; it does not track a volt per octave
Lengthens the output pulse by 2ms per volt, added to the pulse-length knob and clamped between 0.1ms and 20ms
The rectangular wave, switching between -5V and 5V
Note — a trigger arriving during an output pulse is discarded rather than lengthening it, so with the pulse longer than the oscillator's period the rate is governed by the pulse length, not the knob
Note — nothing on the panel is lettered; the artwork carries the module name and no control labels at all

1.why: Ataconso.cpp process(): timbreMs += getVoltage()*(TIMBRE_MS_MAX/10) then clamped to 0.1..20ms

ataconso.notes: The panels in this plugin carry no control lettering, so every line here is written from the maker's source and tooltips. The frequency CV is deliberately not a volt-per-octave input; the source says so in a comment and scales it to the knob's own range instead. The refusal to retrigger while the pulse is high is written into the source on purpose, to copy a real 555 monostable.

compa.notes: The four inputs are given no family: the module compares whatever two voltages are fed to it, and nothing in the code narrows what those are meant to be. The isConnected() guard means an unpatched channel is not simply comparing zero against zero, it is held at 0V.

lines: Two envelope generators, each a linear rise to 10V followed straight away by a linear fall, with a second input that drops the envelope and starts it again
Sets how long channel a takes to climb from 0V to 10V, 0.001 to 5 seconds
Sets how long channel a takes to fall from 10V back to 0V, 0.001 to 5 seconds
Sets how long channel b takes to climb from 0V to 10V, 0.001 to 5 seconds
Sets how long channel b takes to fall from 10V back to 0V, 0.001 to 5 seconds
A rising edge past 1V starts the channel a envelope; an edge arriving while that envelope is already running is discarded
A rising edge past 1V sends the channel a envelope down to 0V at about 10V per second, and a new rise starts when it arrives there
A rising edge past 1V starts the channel b envelope; an edge arriving while that envelope is already running is discarded
A rising edge past 1V sends the channel b envelope down to 0V at about 10V per second, and a new rise starts when it arrives there
The channel a envelope, 0V to 10V
The channel b envelope, 0V to 10V
Note — there is no sustain stage and no gate: the fall begins the instant the rise reaches 10V, whatever the trigger is doing
Note — nothing on the panel is lettered; the artwork carries the module name and no control labels at all
envo.notes: The forced fall is written in the source as a fast ramp, but its step is (10.0f - 0.001f) * sampleTime, which works out at about 10V per second and takes roughly a second from the top. The lines describe the measured rate rather than the source's comment. CanalEnvo.hpp holds the state machine for both channels.

recta.notes: The frequency knob is clamped to four octaves either side of C4 but the volt-per-octave input is not clamped at all, so a large voltage will take an oscillator far above the audible range. The oscillator is a naive phase accumulator with no anti-aliasing.
